books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, February 2, 1848, Articles V and XII (ratified text). Public domain.
stimulus.text:
Article V. The boundary line between the two Republics shall commence in the Gulf of Mexico, three leagues from land, opposite the mouth of the Rio Grande, otherwise called Rio Bravo del Norte . . . from thence up the middle of that river, following the deepest channel, where it has more than one, to the point where it strikes the southern boundary of New Mexico . . . The southern and western limits of New Mexico, mentioned in the article, are those laid down in the map entitled "Map of the United Mexican States, as organized and defined by various acts of the Congress of said republic, and constructed according to the best authorities. Revised edition. Published at New York, in 1847, by J. Disturnell," of which map a copy is added to this treaty, bearing the signatures and seals of the undersigned Plenipotentiaries.

Article XII. In consideration of the extension acquired by the boundaries of the United States, as defined in the fifth article of the present treaty, the Government of the United States engages to pay to that of the Mexican Republic the sum of fifteen millions of dollars.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The treaty settled the war, but it most directly created which of the following new problems for the United States?

options.text: A war with Britain over the Oregon boundary.
options.misconception: The Oregon boundary had already been settled with Britain by treaty in 1846, before this treaty.

options.text: A rebellion by American settlers in Texas against Mexican rule, like the one in 1836.
options.misconception: The Texas revolt happened in 1836, a decade before this treaty, and Texas was already a state.

options.text: A demand by Mexico for the return of Florida.
options.misconception: Florida had been American since 1819, and Mexico never claimed it.

options.text: A national argument over whether slavery would be allowed in the vast new territory.

rationales.A: Oregon was settled with Britain in 1846; this treaty raised no new British dispute.
rationales.B: The Texas revolt was a decade old, and Texas was already a state by 1848.
rationales.C: Florida was not part of this war or this treaty.
rationales.D: The treaty added California and the Southwest, and the question of slavery there split the country — the Wilmot Proviso, the Free-Soil Party, and the Compromise of 1850 all followed.
rationales.general:
1. Count what the treaty added: California, Nevada, Utah, and parts of four more states.
2. Ask the question every acre raised: would slavery be allowed there?
3. Trace the fallout. The Proviso, the Free-Soil Party, and the Compromise of 1850 all grew from that one question.
Remember: winning land can be easier than governing it — the treaty ended a war with Mexico and opened a fight at home.
